# Machine Testimony

> An independent research programme on whether what an automated system says
> about its own reasoning and actions can be verified by someone who was not
> there. Machine testimony is what a system says about what it believed, what
> it was told, what it decided and who allowed it. Testimony is not evidence
> until someone else can check it, so this programme publishes the formats,
> validators and benchmarks that make the checking possible, and implements
> everything it publishes.

The question is not new. In Machine Testimony (126 Yale L.J. 1972, 2017) Andrea
Roth argued that information conveyed by a machine should carry testimonial
safeguards, and worked through what those would have to be: credibility testing
through design and operation protocols, disclosure and access, authentication
and reliability rules, impeachment, and corroboration. This programme takes that
as the brief and builds the parts of it that are engineering.

A good deal of current work goes into receipts: signed, hash chained records
proving an entry has not been altered since it was written. That is worth doing
and settles less than it appears to, because integrity protects the entry rather
than the claim inside it. A record can be cryptographically perfect and
factually false. The harder questions sit underneath: what the system believed
when it decided and on what evidence, what contradicted it and whether the
losing side is still in the record, what happened to conclusions resting on a
premise that was later withdrawn, and whether a human approval came from a
second party or from the acting agent under another name.

## Working papers

- [Working Paper No. 1: Popularity Is Not Association](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22286050) (deposited and archived, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22286050; also readable at https://machinetestimony.org/papers/wp1/) (September 2026, Troy Clifford): a belief-forming rule audited against 19,668 Big Five respondents whose correlation structure this programme did not choose. It recovered the dataset's known five-factor structure at 0.185 against a chance rate of 0.184, meaning it was measuring how common a claim was rather than whether two claims were associated. Requiring the Wilson lower bound of a pair's rate to clear the consequent's own base rate took recovery to 0.875, on 94 per cent fewer regularities that covered more claims than before. A second defect is reported in the same paper: confidence at birth was a linear score being read as a probability, scoring Brier skill -0.689 against always predicting the base rate; repaired, it reaches -0.003, which is parity with that baseline and not better than it, and the paper says so explicitly. Also reports the repaired system's behaviour at volume and retracts an earlier finding that the first defect had caused. Text CC BY 4.0; harnesses are runnable in the reference implementation and the external dataset is not redistributed.

## Conformance census

- [Census No. 1: What Eight Agent Systems Record About What They Did](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22290922) (deposited and archived, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22290922; this version doi:10.5281/zenodo.22290923; also readable at https://machinetestimony.org/census/2026-09/) (4 September 2026, Troy Clifford): eight agent memory and agent framework systems read at pinned commits and assessed against the four Testimony Record conformance levels: OMEM, mem0, Graphiti, LangGraph, CrewAI, the OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen and Letta Code. Twenty requirements drawn from the published levels and restated as capability questions, so a system holding the required information in its own format is judged on whether it holds the information rather than on whether it uses this format. Three findings hold across every system but the reference implementation. Four of the eight gate a consequential action behind a human decision and none records who made it; the one possible exception is recorded as undetermined because its approval record sits in a server that could not be read. None cleanly records that data was destroyed, and the two partial cases fail in opposite directions: one writes the deleted text into its own deletion record, the other keeps it in git history and on every mirror. The fourth level, showing that a past record has not altered, is absent outright in six of eight. Graphiti and LangGraph each meet four of five at the first level and fail only on recording destruction, both having arrived there for reasons unrelated to this specification. Every verdict cites a file and line at a full forty character commit, so a system that later gains a missing capability has not made the finding false: the assessment was of a named tree, and a change produces a new assessment beside the old one rather than an edit. A published manifest digests every assessment and the questions they were scored against. Text CC BY 4.0; the assessments and the rules that reject a careless one are in the reference implementation under benchmarks/census.

## Published work

- [The Testimony Record](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-clifford-testimony-record/): a format for what a system believed, what contradicted it, what it tried to do and who approved it, with four conformance levels TR-1 to TR-4 so a system can be placed rather than described. Specification text CC BY 4.0, schema MIT, free to implement in any language.
- [The reference validator](https://github.com/troybrandonc-bit/machine-testimony): one file, Python standard library only, no network. Copy it into your own repository and run it in your own CI. A conformance claim the listener cannot check is an adjective.
- [The implementations register](https://infrastructure.omem-cloud.com/spec/testimony-record/implementations/): which systems emit records that pass the validator and at what level. Entries follow a checked record, never a self-report.
- [The commons corpus](https://infrastructure.omem-cloud.com/commons/): regularities in human working behaviour as counts over populations, contributed by installations that opted in, holding no fact about any person. CC BY 4.0, with a dataset card that states what it does not cover.
- The Witness benchmark: six properties a memory system either has or does not, checked by a runnable harness. No fabrication, retraction honoured, disagreement visible, identities kept apart, conclusions die with their premises, every memory sourced.
- The calibration benchmark: whether a system's confidence about a person tracks how often it turns out right, scored by Brier skill against the base rate, and reporting nothing rather than a flattering number when the record is too thin to measure.
- [The claims ledger](https://infrastructure.omem-cloud.com/claims/): every load-bearing sentence next to the executable statement that would go red if it stopped being true.

## Regulatory reference

- [Evidencing human oversight under the EU AI Act](https://machinetestimony.org/eu-ai-act/): Articles 12, 14, 15, 26 and 72 mapped to what a record has to contain to answer them, where the prEN 18229 harmonised standards series has reached, and the two technical comments this programme submitted on Part 3. States plainly that it is not legal advice, that no part of prEN 18229 is cited in the Official Journal and so none carries a presumption of conformity, and that certification to ISO/IEC 42001 is not conformity with the Act.
- [The duty to explain is seven times wider than the duty to record](https://machinetestimony.org/explaining/) (deposited, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22658916): Article 86 gives an affected person the right to the main elements of a decision an AI system took part in, across seven of the eight Annex III areas, everything but critical infrastructure. Article 12(3) specifies what a log must contain for one of them, remote biometric identification, which is also the only place the Act requires the record to name the humans who checked. Ten deployed systems read against what answering would take: two can say where a stored fact came from by following a link, and eight cannot say afterwards that anything was ever in dispute. Article 86 was not deferred by the digital omnibus, which moved Chapter III Sections 1 to 3; whether it can be invoked before December 2027 is arguable and the page declines to assert it, because the asymmetry is the same on either reading.
- [Everyone requires the log. Everyone requires the log. One row of Annex III requires it to name who approved](https://machinetestimony.org/obligation/) (deposited, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22658916): the EU AI Act, the ForHumanity certification criteria, the CoSAI Risk Map and the NIST AI RMF read against four questions. All three that specify what a record must contain require one to be kept; only one requires it to name the person who authorised an action, and none requires it to be capable of being shown unaltered by anyone other than its author. The Act writes that requirement exactly once: Article 12(3)(d) obliges the logs of a remote biometric identification system under Annex III point 1(a) to identify the natural persons who verified the result, pointing at Article 14(5) and its two-person rule. Every other high-risk system falls under Article 12(2), which specifies no content at all. The drafters knew the requirement was needed, knew how to word it, and confined it to one row, which is a harder finding to explain away than an oversight. ISO/IEC 42001 has no row because its text is paywalled. NIST is marked not applicable because a framework that deliberately specifies no controls is not failing to specify one.
- [Does the approver see the arguments that execute](https://machinetestimony.org/approval-binding/): six agent frameworks read at pinned commits on whether the arguments a person was shown can change between approval and execution. One binds them, one supplies a mechanism, two do not, and two have no approval pause at all. The same defect is open as an issue in three of them, filed by three people who do not cite each other.
- [Recording who approved](https://machinetestimony.org/approvals/): what an approval has to carry for it to be attributable afterwards, and why an identity taken from run state rather than from the authentication layer identifies the wrong person.
- [Check a record](https://machinetestimony.org/check/): drop a record in a browser and see the level it reaches and every check behind it. The validator runs in the page and nothing is uploaded.
- [Review your own records](https://machinetestimony.org/review/): drop a file of the records a system already writes, in whatever shape it writes them, and see which of the four questions those rows can answer: who approved a consequential action, whether that was a person rather than the agent itself, what the system tried and did not do, and whether the file has changed since it was written. It runs in the page and nothing is uploaded or stored, which is the only footing on which anyone can run it over a client's log. It reports the shape of the rows it was given and concludes nothing about the system that wrote them, and prints that limit with every finding. The same finding comes out of spec/testimony_convert.py at the command line and the build fails if the two disagree.
- [Assess a system yourself](https://machinetestimony.org/assess/): the rubric, harness and method are CC BY 4.0 and MIT with commercial use intended. An auditor can run these twenty requirements against a client's supplier and charge for it without asking anybody. Every verdict cites evidence, including absence, which must cite where the assessor looked.
- [Proving a log was not altered](https://machinetestimony.org/tamper-evidence/): what append-only storage, hash chains, signatures, RFC 3161 timestamps and transparency logs each prove, and against whom. The distinction that matters is whether a scheme detects an edit by an outsider or by the operator who wrote the record; most detect only the first. Runnable commands, and what none of them prove.
- [Questions to ask your AI supplier](https://machinetestimony.org/ask/): eight questions about what a system records, with what a real answer looks like and what a soft yes sounds like. Free to send as your own, with no attribution asked. Six of the eight assessed systems that take actions could not say which person approved one.
- [The register](https://machinetestimony.org/register/): which agent systems record what, standing rather than dated, every verdict citing a file and a line at a pinned commit. A wrong verdict is fixed by a pull request against the subject file, not by argument. The author's own implementation is one row and carries no evidential weight. Each row links to that system's own page, carrying every verdict, the reasoning behind it and a link to each cited line at the pinned commit.
- [Implementing it](https://machinetestimony.org/implement/): a single-file emitter with no dependencies, and 57 records with the verdict each should get, so an implementer can tell when they are finished without asking. Conformance means reaching the same verdict, not printing the same sentences. For a system that already writes records of its own, testimony_convert.py is the shorter path: declare which of your fields mean what and it builds what it can and names every required field it had no value for, which is a measurement of your format rather than advice about it. It never supplies a value it was not given, so a field your records cannot fill is reported as missing and the row is not converted, rather than becoming a conforming record that answers a question your system could not.
- [A record you can check without us](https://machinetestimony.org/anchor/): a published Testimony Record whose digest is signed by a Time Stamp Authority, with the three commands that verify it. None of the three is ours. The page also records what the validator was not checking until 5 September 2026, when the level called Verifiable could be reached with a digest of sixty-four zeros.
- [Proposing a change](https://machinetestimony.org/changes/): how somebody other than the editor gets a defect fixed or a change into the specification, what is accepted and what is not.

## What this is not

- Not a certification body. This programme publishes formats and the tools to check them. It audits nobody and issues no certificates. The validator is public so any conformance claim can be checked by the person hearing it, including every claim made here.
- One member. A research programme run by one person, not an institution with a staff.
- Every implementation is by this programme's editor. Two validators, Python and TypeScript, written separately and checked against each other, and two emitters: OMEM, which is the reference implementation and is not the specification, and testimony-langgraph, which depends on LangGraph and on nothing of ours. No implementation by another party is known. A format implemented only by its author is a proposal rather than a standard, and an implementation by somebody else is worth more to this work than anything else on the list.
- It does not decide what is true. Nothing published here reads two accounts and concludes which is right. The record keeps both sides, says which evidence each rests on, and leaves the judgement to a person.

## Reference implementation

- [OMEM](https://github.com/troybrandonc-bit/Omem): MIT licensed, self hosted, zero runtime dependencies. `pip install omem-infrastructure && omem-server`.
- [Documentation](https://infrastructure.omem-cloud.com/)

Editor: Troy Clifford. Operated by Garnet Taurus Ltd.
